title: Word sort order when computing document embeddings
description:
Hi! I've been working through this lovely book (even though I'm a few years late to the party) and have a question (and possible issue?) to chapter 5. In the code below, I've lightly modified the PMI -> word embeddings -> document embeddings workflow by limiting the number of complaints analyzed to 1000, changing the occurrence threshold, and adding some scratch code at the end.

Specifically, I am interested in the logic behind the `word_matrix %*% embedding_matrix` step to create a document embedding (end of 5.3). My matrix algebra is a little rusty, but what I think is happening (or at least should be happening) is for each dimension and for each document sum( # of times a word appears * embedding value). As written, that'll create 100 columns per document and those values represent the document embedding. 

If I'm correct, shouldn't the columns in word_matrix should have the same arrangement as the rows in embedding_matrix? That is, shouldn't `all(colnames(word_matrix) == rownames(embedding_matrix))` be `TRUE`?

In `word_matrix2` and `embedding_matrix2` (and `word_matrix3` and `embedding_matrix3`) I sort things so that condition is TRUE, but I don't think the code as written in the book makes that guarantee. I also compute things for a specific complaint via the `bootleg` object.

```
# Should only take a minute or two to run
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)

complaints <- read_csv("data/complaints.csv.gz")

tidy_complaints <- complaints %>%
  slice(sample(seq_len(nrow(complaints)), 1000)) |> 
  select(complaint_id, consumer_complaint_narrative) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, consumer_complaint_narrative) %>%
  add_count(word) %>%
  filter(n >= 10) %>%
  select(-n)

nested_words <- tidy_complaints %>%
  nest(words = c(word))

slide_windows <- function(tbl, window_size) {
  skipgrams <- slider::slide(
    tbl,
    ~.x,
    .after = window_size - 1,
    .step = 1,
    .complete = TRUE
  )
  
  safe_mutate <- safely(mutate)
  
  out <- map2(skipgrams,
              1:length(skipgrams),
              ~ safe_mutate(.x, window_id = .y))
  
  out %>%
    transpose() %>%
    pluck("result") %>%
    compact() %>%
    bind_rows()
}

library(widyr)
library(furrr)

plan(multisession(workers = 3))  ## for parallel processing

tidy_pmi <- nested_words %>%
  mutate(words = future_map(words, slide_windows, 4L)) %>%
  unnest(words) %>%
  unite(window_id, complaint_id, window_id) %>%
  pairwise_pmi(word, window_id)

#save(tidy_pmi, file = "data/tidy_pmi.rda", compress = "xz")

tidy_word_vectors <- tidy_pmi %>%
  widely_svd(
    item1, item2, pmi,
    nv = 100, maxit = 1000
  )

tidy_word_vectors

word_matrix <- tidy_complaints %>%
  count(complaint_id, word) %>%
  cast_sparse(complaint_id, word, n)

embedding_matrix <- tidy_word_vectors %>%
  cast_sparse(item1, dimension, value)

doc_matrix <- word_matrix %*% embedding_matrix

# With sorting
word_matrix2 <- tidy_complaints %>%
  count(complaint_id, word) %>%
  arrange(word) |>
  cast_sparse(complaint_id, word, n)

embedding_matrix2 <- tidy_word_vectors %>%
  arrange(item1, dimension) |>
  cast_sparse(item1, dimension, value)

table(colnames(word_matrix2) == rownames(embedding_matrix2))


doc_matrix2 = word_matrix2 %*% embedding_matrix2

example_row = tidy_complaints$complaint_id[1] |> as.character()

a = doc_matrix[which(rownames(doc_matrix) == example_row),] |> as.numeric()
b = doc_matrix2[which(rownames(doc_matrix2) == example_row),] |> as.numeric()

a == b

# Bootleg matrix multiplication
word_matrix3 <- tidy_complaints %>%
  count(complaint_id, word) %>%
  filter(complaint_id == example_row)

embedding_matrix3 <- tidy_word_vectors %>%
  arrange(item1, dimension) 

bootleg = left_join(word_matrix3, embedding_matrix3, by = join_by('word' == 'item1'))
bootleg = bootleg |> mutate(val = value * n) |> group_by(complaint_id, dimension) |> summarize(score_bl = sum(val))
bootleg = bootleg |> mutate(score_orig = a, score_sort = b)
```

title: Chapter 6 code is extremely slow
description:
Hello. Thank you for the nice book. Similar to what was posted in issue https://github.com/EmilHvitfeldt/smltar/issues/177, my collaborator and I had difficulty running the example you provided in the book, so we only had to take a subset of the data. Since it was not mentioned in the book that the example may potentially run slow, we thought it would be worth highlighting this. If you execute the same approach with `quanteda`, it's 4-6 times faster (and the gap increases) for the same operation. You can see that below.

```R
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)
library(textrecipes)
library(scotus)
library(tidytext)
library(lexicon)
library(quanteda)

# `textrecipes` approach mentioned in the book
set.seed(1234)

book_demo <- function() {
  scotus_split <- scotus_filtered[1:500,] %>%
    mutate(year = as.numeric(year),
           text = str_remove_all(text, "'")) %>%
    initial_split()
  
  scotus_train <- training(scotus_split)
  scotus_test <- testing(scotus_split)
  
  scotus_rec <- recipe(year ~ text, data = scotus_train) %>%
    step_tokenize(text) %>%
    step_tokenfilter(text, max_tokens = 100) %>%
    step_tfidf(text) %>%
    step_normalize(all_predictors())
  scotus_prep <- prep(scotus_rec)
}


# significant performance different doing the same with quanteda
tweets.cp <- corpus(scotus_filtered[1:500,], text_field = "text")

quanteda_demo <- function() {
  tweets.tok <- tokens(tweets.cp, remove_url = TRUE) %>%
    tokens(
      remove_punct = TRUE,
      remove_symbols = TRUE,
      remove_numbers = TRUE,
      split_hyphens = TRUE,
      what = "word1"
    ) ## option what="word1" => removes hastags and tags symbols (@, #, etc.)
  tweets.tok <- tweets.tok %>% tokens_tolower() %>%
    tokens_remove(stop_words$word, min_nchar = 3) %>%
    tokens_replace(pattern = hash_lemmas$token, replacement = hash_lemmas$lemma)
  tweets.dfm <- dfm(tweets.tok) %>% dfm_tfidf()
}

system.time({
  book_demo()
})
#   user  system elapsed 
#  25.52    0.25   25.83 

system.time({
  quanteda_demo()
})
#   user  system elapsed 
#   8.11    0.11    5.65 
```

title: Linguistic terminology
description:
Hi Emil and Julia,

Big fan here. I am using this book with my graduate course 'Digital Text Analysis' at UT Austin. 

I wanted to make a correction to your brief exposition on morphology in chapter 1, where you write 

`Danish words such as “brandbil” (fire truck), “politibil” (police car), and “lastbil” (truck) all contain the morpheme “bil” (car) and start with prefixes denoting the type of car. `

Please note that _brand-, politi-,_ etc. in these examples are _not_ prefixes. Rather, _brandbil_ and the other examples are (endocentric) noun-noun [compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compound_(linguistics)). 

A prefix is a bound morpheme that cannot be a word on its own, but in these compounds you have two potentially independent morphemes.

--Lars Hinrichs

title: Chapter 4 Stemming Code Error
description:
Thanks for writing the book, as I was working through the chapter I noticed that the **ungroup** function has missing brackets.

## code 1
`tidy_by_lang %>%
  inner_join(stopword_df) %>%
  mutate(data = map2(
    data, two_letter, ~ anti_join(.x, get_stopwords(language = .y)))
  ) %>%
  unnest(data) %>%
  mutate(stem = wordStem(word, language = language)) %>%

title: Need to correct info about articles in German
description:
In [Stop words in languages other than English](https://smltar.com/stopwords.html) there are some mistakes in the table about German articles. From an email I got:

> Please note that "keine" is the negative indefinite article (not the plural) in German.  I am not a native speaker of German, so I won't try to correct your table - but I do know that this is incorrect (the plural of an indefinite article is a bit puzzling anyway - I am not sure that such a thing exists).

And more: 

> There is a plural indefinite article in German - but  only  in the negative. So we would get
>
> sing: ein Fisch       negative: kein Fisch.       (a fish/no fish)
> plural: Fische.        negative: keine Fische    (fishes/no fishes)
>
> So the plural indefinite article in German seems to be a zero - as it is in English.

Gotta figure this one out! 👀
